title: Fear not: Maya spared from the fire
hookLine: a builder runs out of a burning forest, and Arjuna says: don't be afraid
carry: abhaya: protect the one who asks for refuge

cards: A forest is on fire, and a man runs out of it. He's Maya, an asura and a master builder, with the flames at his back. Krishna raises his discus.

Maya cries out to Arjuna to save him, and Arjuna answers: don't be afraid. Those words save his life. And the next book of the Mahabharata, the Sabha Parva, the book of the hall, opens with the man they saved.

teach.b: First, how the family got here. After the wedding, the Pandavas go back to Hastinapura. Dhritarashtra gives them half the kingdom, the wild half, and there they build a city, Indraprastha.

Then Krishna and Arjuna help the fire god Agni burn the Khandava forest, guarding its edges so nothing escapes. It's a hard chapter: the text names only a handful who survive. Maya is one, because of one sentence.

Don't be afraid. And Krishna stays his hand. Those words are one of the great gifts in Hindu dharma, and the gift has a name: abhaya, fearlessness, the gift of safety to someone who comes asking for refuge.

In the epics, protecting the one who asks for shelter is counted a high duty, even when he's from the enemy's side; in the Ramayana, Rama takes in Ravana's own brother when he comes for refuge. And you've seen abhaya.
On many Hindu images, Ganesha, Durga, Shiva as the dancer, one hand is raised, palm open, facing you. It doesn't mean stop.
It's the abhaya mudra: don't be afraid.

teach.h: SHELTER FOR THE ONE WHO ASKS.
teach.b: Many Hindus read it two ways: a promise from God to you, and a job for you.
The worried cousin who needs a couch, the classmate nobody sits with: abhaya means you say 'you're safe here' first and ask questions later. Then Maya, safe, wants to repay Arjuna.
Arjuna won't take anything; in paraphrase, be a friend to me.
So Krishna asks for a gift for someone else: build a hall for Yudhishthira, one no one could copy. That's this stretch's word, sabha: a hall, and the assembly that meets in it.

how: The raised open palm on many Hindu murtis is the abhaya mudra, the gesture that says 'fear not'. Hindu tradition places the Pandavas' city of Indraprastha near present-day Delhi.

o: a city built on wild land cleared by fire
a hall, and the assembly that gathers in it
a fire sacrifice that crowns a king over kings

games.q: the fire and the promise — tap the pairs.
p: asks for a hall for Yudhishthira

s: Arjuna asked Maya to build the hall
he refused any reward; Krishna asked for the hall, for Yudhishthira.
the raised open palm on a Hindu murti means stop
it's the abhaya mudra: don't be afraid.
Arjuna promised safety to Maya, an asura
protecting the one who asks for refuge is a high duty, even for someone from the other side.

games.q: you're Arjuna. the forest is burning, Krishna's discus is raised, and an asura you don't know cries out to you for help. what do you do?
o: let Krishna decide; he's an asura.
ask what he'll give you first.
games.why: 'don't be afraid.' he gives safety first and asks nothing. that's abhaya. when Maya later offers a reward, Arjuna refuses it.

practice: Raise your right hand, palm open and facing out, the way it's raised on so many Hindu images. Hold it there for a few breaths, and bring to mind someone who's afraid right now.
If you pray, ask God to be their shelter; if you don't, simply wish them safety. Then lower your hand and think of one way you could be someone's 'don't be afraid' this week.

wordCard.voice: Sabha. A hall, and the assembly that gathers in it. Today, the hall at Indraprastha is promised by a builder who heard Arjuna say: don't be afraid.

orig.note: Sanskrit abhaya: fearlessness, freedom from fear. The abhaya mudra is the raised open palm that says don't be afraid.

carryVoice: Your line: abhaya: protect the one who asks for refuge. One raised hand says it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Viduragamana and Rajya-labha Parvas (the return to Hastinapura; half the kingdom; Indraprastha built at Khandavaprastha)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Khandava-daha Parva (Maya spared from the burning forest)
Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, opening sections (Maya offers service; Arjuna declines; Krishna asks for a hall for Yudhishthira)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Rama grants refuge to Vibhishana, Ravana's brother)
